abstract: Energy-based models have shown promising properties for domain-specific tasks but remain challenging in modeling general-purpose scenarios. To bridge this gap, we design Energy-Based Foundation Models (EBFMs) for general language modeling. EBFMs integrate energy steering and token generation within a single architecture to leverage the energy-guided search to refine token generation. Specifically, EBFMs first optimize a latent state over the energy landscape, then leverages the refined latent state for token generation. By performing such energy-guided pre-training on large-scale corpora, EBFMs learn generally effective energy landscape where favorable tokens correspond to lower energy values. To explore the scaling behavior of EBFMs, we pre-train EBFMs on three large-scale corpora, then evaluate across 26 downstream tasks spanning a broad range of domains. Our results demonstrate that EBFMs have promising scaling behaviors with increasing model size and training data, and outperform GPTs on most downstream tasks. These findings highlight EBFMs as a promising architecture for large-scale pre-training and general purpose problem solving. We fully release the model weights and training infrastructure to enable the community to completely reproduce and extend our results.

sections.body: The paper states that energy-based models have been designed and evaluated within single tasks or domains, and their generality is largely unexplored. It proposes Energy-Based Foundation Models (EBFMs), with an energy head and a generative head in one architecture, so that energy evaluation can refine token generation. The authors pre-train EBFMs on three large-scale corpora, Fineweb, Climbmix, and DCLM, and evaluate them zero-shot on 26 downstream tasks. The stated claims are promising scaling with model size and training data and consistent advantages over GPTs. The training recipe, infrastructure, and model weights are said to be released.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing energy-based models are limited to single domains, so this paper proposes energy-based foundation models for general language modeling.

sections.body: This section defines the inputs and outputs of the model. A context sequence x and a latent variable z of embedding dimension D are the inputs. The energy head is a linear layer that outputs a scalar energy score. The generative head is an embedding layer with softmax operations that outputs tokens from the vocabulary. Both heads share one Transformer backbone, so energy evaluation and token generation sit in a single architecture. The section also states that enumerating the full token space to find the lowest-energy solution is computationally infeasible, which is why energy evaluation is used to refine generation instead.
sections.heading: Preliminary
sections.headline: Preliminaries define an energy head and a generative head that share one Transformer backbone.

sections.body: Energy steering starts from a Gaussian latent state and takes K gradient-descent steps on the energy, with model parameters fixed. The paper uses these steps to approximate the exact minimization and omits the noise used in standard sampling, because deterministic updates were more stable in large-scale pre-training. The steered latent state then feeds the generative head, which predicts the next tokens. For training, the paper runs steering at every position at once through a re-designed attention mask and positional indices, and minimizes a negative log-likelihood loss on the next tokens. Table 1 lists MCMC Steps as 1.
sections.heading: Energy-based Foundation Models
sections.headline: Energy steering refines a latent state by gradient descent on the energy, and training runs this for all positions in parallel.

sections.body: The section reports pre-training on Fineweb, Climbmix, and DCLM at depths of 12, 20, and 26 layers, with hidden width set by a GPT-2 configuration. On Climbmix, the 12-, 20-, and 26-layer EBFMs match GPTs trained on 7B tokens after 4.5B, 3.5B, and 5.1B tokens. Zero-shot accuracy on 19 question-answering tasks is reported in Table 2, where EBFMs significantly outperform GPTs on most tasks. In zero-shot generation after pre-training on OpenWebText, EBFMs reach an average BPB of 1.35 versus 1.37 for GPTs. The authors describe the advantage as growing at larger scales.
sections.heading: Evaluation Results
sections.headline: EBFMs match GPT validation error with fewer training tokens and outperform GPTs on most zero-shot question-answering tasks.

sections.body: The section gives where to find the training infrastructure and logs on GitHub and the model weights on Hugging Face. It states that all datasets used are publicly available and linked in the released code. The authors state that they hope the community can reproduce the results and explore energy-based foundation models further. No new experimental evidence is given in this section.
sections.heading: Open-source Release
sections.headline: Training infrastructure, logs, and model weights are released publicly, with datasets linked in the released code.

sections.body: The largest configuration tested is d26 with 1.03B parameters. The text states that pre-training efficiency is a major bottleneck. Current training relies on distributed data parallelism, where each GPU holds a full backbone. Existing model-parallel frameworks such as FSDP, Megatron-LM, and DeepSpeed ZeRO do not readily support the second-order differentiation that EBM training requires. As a result, a model cannot be easily sharded, which limits model size to the memory of a single H200 GPU. The second limitation is block-wise generation, which the authors describe as an important direction for future work.
sections.heading: Limitations under Current Ecosystem
sections.headline: Scaling is limited because current parallelism tools lack second-order gradient support, and block-wise generation is future work.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the contribution: EBFMs perform energy steering on hidden states during inference to guide token generation toward lower-energy outputs. The authors describe parallel energy steering as the means of efficient pre-training on three large-scale corpora. They report promising scaling performance with increased model size and training cost across multiple evaluation settings and 19 downstream tasks. The authors claim these findings show substantial potential for general-purpose tasks. Model weights and infrastructure are released to allow full reproduction. The section offers no new numerical results.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Energy steering shows promising scaling across 19 downstream tasks, and the weights and infrastructure are fully released.

sections.body: The section lists directions the authors invite the community to pursue. Supervised fine-tuning on domain data, such as scientific reasoning, code generation, and finance, is one. Efficient inference and training is another, because EBFMs differ architecturally from GPTs, which makes methods such as GPTQ, Flash Attention, and Page Attention hard to apply. The third is training infrastructure that supports model sharding across GPUs and memory-efficient higher-order gradients, comparable with FSDP and Megatron-LM. The section does not report new experimental results.
sections.heading: Future Directions
sections.headline: Suggested future work covers supervised fine-tuning, efficient inference and training algorithms, and distributed training infrastructure.
